results.title: Ad frequency: how often people should see your ad
results.markdown:
Title: Ad frequency: how often people should see your ad

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/ad-frequency-small-business

Published Time: 2026-11-09T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Ad frequency has no single right number, but the research points to a range. Meta’s brand-lift analysis found a cap of 2 impressions per person per week captured 95% of the potential purchase-intent lift. A CTV study found purchase intent fell as one viewer’s exposures in a session climbed toward six.

Start with a modest weekly cap and adjust when fatigue signals appear.

Ad frequency is the average number of times one person sees your ad during a set period, usually a day, a week or the length of a campaign. If 1,000 people saw your ad 3,000 times in a week, your weekly frequency is 3. Because it is an average, some people saw the ad once and others saw it six or seven times.

A frequency cap is the ceiling: the most times the platform will show your ad to one person in that period. Before serving an ad, the platform checks whether that person has reached the cap and skips them if they have. Many platforms also offer a second control. [Epom’s guide to ad frequency](https://epom.com/blog/dsp/ad-frequency-best-practices) separates the cap, which limits how many times, from recency, which sets the minimum gap between views. Improvado gives a programmatic example of a recency cap: one impression per hour.

Frequency is counted in impressions, and an impression is not the same as a view. [Improvado’s frequency capping glossary](https://improvado.io/blog/understanding-frequency-capping) defines an impression as each time an ad is displayed on a screen, whether or not the person noticed it. Your reported frequency can therefore run higher than the number of times someone actually paid attention, and that is one reason the right number varies by format.

## How frequency works on TV, CTV and social

How much control you have depends on how the channel is bought. Traditional linear TV is sold by time slot and program. [Amazon Ads’ linear TV guide](https://advertising.amazon.com/library/guides/linear-tv-advertising) describes advertisers buying commercial time based on expected viewership, with ads running in scheduled program breaks. You choose the shows and dayparts, but you cannot limit how often one household sees your spot. Streaming TV runs on internet-connected devices, and Amazon Ads notes that these platforms add tools such as completion rates and frequency caps.

![Image 1: Woman on a couch at night holding a phone while a television plays in front of her](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/28d1108883e13878d943344747274317731433efff0b1582443c1a3eb0634236.jpg)

| Channel | How you control frequency | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear TV (broadcast, cable, satellite) | Indirectly, through the programs, dayparts and number of spots you buy | No per-person cap; frequency is estimated from ratings |
| Streaming TV (CTV) | Per-viewer or per-household caps where the platform offers them | Caps apply within the platform or buying route you use |
| Facebook and Instagram | A target frequency (impressions per person per week) or a frequency cap, set at campaign or ad set level | Campaign-level and ad set-level controls can’t be combined |
| Google display and programmatic | Hard impression caps per day, week or month; some platforms add lifetime and recency caps | Granularity depends on the platform |

Every cap stops at the edge of one platform. Improvado gives an example: a cap of 3 per day on Google and 3 per day on Facebook can still mean 6 impressions a day for the same person. Neither platform knows about the other, so cross-channel frequency is something you have to estimate yourself. For more detail on streaming TV specifically, see [our CTV frequency guide](https://adwave.com/resources/ctv-ad-frequency-how-many-times).

## What research says about effective frequency

Effective frequency is the number of exposures one person needs within a period before an ad produces the response you want. The [Universal Marketing Dictionary’s definition](https://marketing-dictionary.org/e/effective-frequency/) rests on the assumption that the first few exposures may have little effect and the message starts to influence people only after more of them.

The idea has a long and somewhat shaky history. In [a chapter on what effective frequency means today](https://sk.sagepub.com/book/edvol/the-advertising-business/chpt/what-does-effective-frequency-mean-today), advertising researcher John Philip Jones argues that it is “rooted not so much in research as in common sense.” He notes that Michael Naples’s 1979 book gave the practice academic respectability, but its strongest support came from Colin McDonald’s work, which Jones calls “merely a small-scale experiment” done years earlier in another country. Be skeptical of any single magic number, including the popular rule that people must see an ad three times.

Newer platform research is more useful because it measures specific outcomes. [Meta’s effective frequency study](https://www.facebook.com/business/news/insights/effective-frequency-reaching-full-campaign-potential) found that lift in both ad recall and purchase intent rose with frequency, but at different rates:

*   A cap of 1 per week captured up to 80% of the total potential lift in ad recall.
*   Recall lift slowed sharply after a cap of 1 per week, while purchase-intent lift didn’t start to slow until close to 1.5 per week.
*   A cap of 2 per week captured 95% of the total potential purchase-intent lift.

Meta reads this as support for the idea that bigger behavior changes, such as intent to buy, need more exposures than simple recall.

Streaming TV research shows what happens when frequency goes too high. An MNTN CTV study, reported by Epom, found recall rose from about 64% after one view to 92% after six in a single session, while purchase intent fell 16% over the same range and brand affinity slipped. Taken together, these findings suggest recall is a poor guide to frequency: it keeps climbing after the measures that lead to sales have started to decline.

## Starting caps by channel

Epom has published suggested starting caps per user per week. They are one practitioner’s starting points, not industry rules or measured results, and they are useful mainly as a first setting you then test.

| Channel | Suggested starting cap (per user per week) | Epom’s reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CTV / streaming TV | 4 to 6 per viewer | Ads interrupt the show and few creatives are usually in rotation |
| Facebook and Instagram Feed | 3 to 5 | Fatigue commonly sets in around 6 to 7 on a single creative |
| Facebook and Instagram Stories and Reels | 2 to 4 | Higher-attention format with lower tolerance than Feed |
| Programmatic online video | About 10 | Holds attention, but skippable formats fatigue faster |
| Display, prospecting | 15 to 25 | Banner blindness means people tolerate more exposures |
| Display, retargeting | 10 to 15 (about 3 a day at most) | A smaller pool of people gets overexposed quickly |

The Meta Feed range sits above the 2 per week that Meta’s own brand-lift work found efficient for purchase intent, which is why Epom also notes Meta’s data pointing to about 2 per week for awareness. If your goal is a booked appointment or a sale, the lower end is a sensible place to begin. Our guides to [Facebook advertising for small businesses](https://adwave.com/resources/facebook-advertising-for-small-business) and [display ads for small businesses](https://adwave.com/resources/display-advertising-small-business) cover those channels beyond frequency.

Ad fatigue happens when people see the same ad so often that it stops working. [Criteo’s ad fatigue guide](https://www.criteo.com/blog/ad-fatigue-how-to-detect-and-prevent-it/) lists warning signs worth checking weekly:

![Image 2: Bored man looking away from a television and reaching for the remote](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/8b5846d3052b24a743cf36127f0c1d8480a3b7a5cd3047739d25e369b5f989b1.jpg)

*   Click-through rate falls while impressions hold flat or rise.
*   Cost per click, cost per thousand impressions or cost per acquisition rises with no clear change in the market.
*   Frequency keeps climbing while engagement drops.
*   One creative takes a large share of the spend but underperforms the campaign’s average click-through rate.
*   The same people see the same message several times in a short window, which is common in retargeting.

[Keen Decision Systems’ ad fatigue guide](https://keends.com/blog/ad-fatigue/) adds two more: unique reach that plateaus while impressions keep piling up, and more negative feedback such as skips or hides. Criteo stresses that combined signals matter more than any one metric. A dip in click-through rate on its own could be seasonal. Falling clicks plus rising costs plus rising frequency is a much clearer warning.

results.title: Where ad frequency statistics are heading in 2026
results.markdown:
Title: Where ad frequency statistics are heading in 2026

URL Source: https://www.webtonic.io/blog/frequency-statistics

Published Time: 2026-09-20T14:22:53+00:00

Markdown Content:
**"Avoid ad fatigue" is not a frequency cap - it is a slogan. Platform research from Meta, Nielsen and the IPA all point to a specific range where incremental response starts to bend, and 2026 streaming-ad-load data is making that ceiling harder to control from the advertiser's side alone.** This page collects where the actual numbers sit, by platform and objective.

*   **A frequency cap of 1 per week captures about 80% of ad-recall lift** on Meta.
*   **Purchase-intent lift keeps rising until nearly 1.5 exposures per week**.
*   **Meta's brand-building guidance recommends 2 or more exposures per week** for long-term goals.
*   **CTR decline is commonly reported above roughly 3.5 frequency** in a 7-day window.
*   **Conversion-rate and cost damage is clearer above frequency 5**.
*   **Fewer than half of CMOs surveyed maximize reach before adding frequency**, per the IPA.
*   **Roughly nine in ten CMOs don't cap frequency at all**, per the same 2026 IPA report.
*   **US streaming ad loads rose 18% between January and August 2026**, per Ampere Analysis.
*   **Netflix's ad minutes per hour rose 74% over the same period**.
*   **Average CTV campaign frequency was measured at 7.09 exposures** in a recent benchmark.
*   **Google Ads frames frequency capping as advertiser-set, not a fixed platform number**.
*   **Common practitioner anchors run 2 to 3 exposures/week for Display, 3 to 5 for video recall**.
*   **Layering CTV on linear can lift unique reach by up to 32%**, reducing repeat exposure.
*   **Nielsen research finds reach delivers more ROI than added frequency** once flattening starts.

Meta for Business's effective-frequency research is the most-cited source behind most published Meta frequency caps: it found that a cap of roughly **1 exposure per week** captures about **80%** of total available ad-recall lift, while lift in purchase intent kept climbing until close to **1.5 exposures per week** before slowing meaningfully. Meta's broader guidance on digital advertising's role in long-term brand growth separately recommends aiming for a frequency of **two or more exposures per week** for campaigns built around brand-building rather than short-term recall, which is a materially different target than the 1x recall figure.

The gap between those two numbers is the most common source of confusion in frequency-cap settings: a recall-optimized campaign and a brand-building campaign are optimizing for different curves, and copying one campaign's cap onto the other objective produces either wasted spend or under-exposure.

![Image 1: Bar chart of Meta effective frequency research showing 80 percent of available ad recall lift captured at 1 exposure per week, purchase intent lift continuing to roughly 1.5 exposures per week, and Meta's own 2 or more exposures per week guidance for long-term brand campaigns](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69f25fb5117656a509dd8790/6aafec5d86849ee345856bda_6aafec403a3089f25d0551ba_frequency-statistics-chart-1.webp)

| Meta frequency benchmark | Exposure level | What it optimizes for | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Recall lift capture point | ~1x per week | 80% of available recall lift | Meta for Business |
| Purchase intent lift ceiling | ~1.5x per week | Near-maximal purchase intent lift | Meta for Business |
| Brand-building recommendation | 2x+ per week | Long-term sales through brand-building | Meta for Business |
| Reported CTR decline threshold | ~3.5x in 7 days | Signals creative fatigue setting in | Practitioner analyses of Meta data |
| Reported conversion/cost damage threshold | ~5x in 7 days | Materially worse cost efficiency | Practitioner analyses of Meta data |

The IPA's 2026 ["Go Big or Go Home"](https://ipa.co.uk/knowledge/publications-reports/go-big-or-go-home) report, written by Les Binet and Will Davis, is blunt about the gap between effectiveness evidence and practitioner behavior: fewer than half of surveyed CMOs actually maximize reach before layering on frequency, and roughly **nine in ten** do not cap frequency at all. That runs against the IPA's long-standing effectiveness evidence, built over more than a decade of Databank analysis, that reach against a broader audience typically delivers more incremental value than repeated exposure to an audience already reached - once a campaign's reach curve has started flattening, the marginal exposure is buying frequency, not audience.

Nielsen's own reach-efficiency research reaches a similar conclusion from a different data source: it found that campaigns without deliberate reach management see average frequency climb from four or fewer exposures on smaller campaigns to **six or more** once impression volume scales past 15 million, without a proportional gain in unique audience reached.

| Effectiveness finding (2026) | Figure | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CMOs who maximize reach before frequency | Under half | IPA, Binet & Davis |
| CMOs who don't cap frequency at all | ~90% | IPA, Binet & Davis |
| Frequency at under 15M impressions | 4 or fewer, typical | Nielsen reach-efficiency research |
| Frequency once campaigns exceed 15M impressions | 6 or more, typical | Nielsen reach-efficiency research |
| Share of marketing budget IPA/Medialab estimate misallocated to activation | 30%-40% | IPA / Gartner 2025 cited in report |

Frequency management is not only an advertiser setting anymore. Ampere Analysis data, reported via [Android Authority](https://www.androidauthority.com/streaming-services-more-ads-2026-3708866/), found that average ad loads across major US streaming services rose **18%** between January and August 2026, with Netflix's measured ad minutes per hour up **74%** over the same window even while remaining the lowest-load service in the comparison. Paramount+ now runs roughly nine ad minutes an hour, with Disney+ and Hulu in the 7.5-to-8.5-minute range.

A separate [CTV benchmark referencing Innovid's 2025 measurement](https://clouddosage.com/ctv-ad-repetition-smart-tv-gaming/) put average campaign frequency at **7.09** exposures across a footprint of more than 95 million US households, well above the 1x-to-2x range Meta's research ties to maximal recall lift. As overall platform ad load rises, an advertiser's own frequency cap controls only their share of exposure - the household's total ad exposure across every advertiser on that platform keeps climbing regardless.

![Image 2: Horizontal bar chart of 2026 US streaming ad minutes per hour by service showing Paramount Plus near 9 minutes, Disney Plus and Hulu between 7.5 and 8.5 minutes, and Netflix under 2.5 minutes despite a 74 percent year-to-date increase](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69f25fb5117656a509dd8790/6aafec5d86849ee345856be0_6aafec41a2ae0ba1ec0e145b_frequency-statistics-chart-2.webp)

[Google Ads Help](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6034106) documents frequency capping as a setting the advertiser configures at the campaign, ad group or ad level for Display and video campaigns, and explicitly notes that only viewable impressions count toward the cap for Display - it does not publish one universal recommended number. Practitioner guidance built on top of that framework commonly anchors **2 to 3** exposures per week for Display and Demand Gen campaigns, and **3 to 5** per week for video campaigns built around recall, then adjusts from the account's own frequency-distribution reporting after roughly two weeks of delivery data.

The practical difference from Meta's framework is that Google Ads treats the cap as a delivery control to be tuned per account, while Meta publishes a specific researched curve advertisers can start from directly - meaning a Google Display cap benefits more from an early testing window than a Meta cap does.

| Platform / format | Common 2026 frequency anchor | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meta, recall-optimized | ~1x per week | Meta effective-frequency research |
| Meta, brand-building | 2x+ per week | Meta long-term brand growth guidance |
| Google Display / Demand Gen | 2-3x per week | Practitioner convention, no fixed platform number |
| Video, recall objective | 3-5x per week | Practitioner convention |
| CTV, measured average | ~7.09x per campaign | Innovid-class CTV benchmark |

![Image 3: Branded matrix graphic comparing recommended ad frequency ranges across Meta recall, Meta brand-building, Google Display, video recall and CTV, each tied to its published 2026 source and the risk of exceeding it](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69f25fb5117656a509dd8790/6aafec5d86849ee345856bdd_6aafec414396721fb9959901_frequency-statistics-framework.webp)

Platform-reported frequency curves are built from short campaign windows; the longer-run academic literature on advertising repetition adds a nuance those windows miss. A widely-cit

results.title: What is Frequency Capping: How to Optimize Ad Exposure
results.markdown:
Title: What is Frequency Capping: How to Optimize Ad Exposure

URL Source: https://www.aidigital.com/blog/frequency-capping

Markdown Content:
When the same audience sees the same **ads** too often, performance starts to suffer: click-through rates decline, impressions are wasted, and useful brand exposure can turn into brand irritation. In Optimove’s **2026 Marketing Fatigue Report**, **83% of consumers said they unsubscribe due to repeated offers because they know they will see them again on other channels**, showing how quickly repetition becomes a cross-channel customer experience problem. Frequency capping helps solve this tension by controlling how often people see an ad within a specific period, protecting campaign efficiency without cutting off valuable reach. For marketers managing budgets across CTV, display, social, audio, and programmatic environments, this guide explains how to use a frequency cap strategically to reduce fatigue, improve media efficiency, and manage ad exposure across fragmented digital channels.

**Frequency capping** has become harder to manage because media exposure no longer happens inside one clean channel. The same customer may see a brand’s **ads** on Connected TV, scroll past them on social media, encounter display placements on publisher sites, and hear the same campaign in digital audio—all within the same day.

eMarketer estimates that U.S. digital ad spending will surpass [**$300 billion in 2026**](https://www.emarketer.com/content/us-ad-spending-2026), with Connected TV alone expected to exceed **$40 billion** in spend. That expansion creates more opportunities for reach, but also more risk of cumulative overexposure when platforms manage frequency separately.

The problem is not that advertisers lack a frequency cap. It is that most caps are still enforced inside individual platforms. A campaign may control exposure in a DSP, Meta, Google, Amazon, or a CTV buying platform, yet still fail to understand how often the same audience is being reached across all of them combined. That fragmentation can lead to saturation, wasted impressions, declining engagement, and a worse customer experience.

For enterprise advertisers, effective frequency management now requires a cross-channel view of exposure, not just platform-level controls. The goal is no longer simply to limit impressions inside one campaign; it is to coordinate reach, repetition, creative rotation, and measurement across the entire media mix so budgets work harder without exhausting the audience.

![Image 1: Chart of projected 2026 U.S. net digital ad revenues by company, led by Meta at $100.86B and Alphabet at $94.81B, with 14 companies expected to exceed $2B.](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69a18e5fa71a1769128536f9/6a871e957764e2d659fc1d5d_ad-revenues-by-company-branded.webp)

_Campanies will have over $2B in net digital ad revenues in 2026 (Source)._

**Frequency capping** is the practice of limiting how many times an individual user, household, or audience segment is exposed to the same advertisement within a defined period. A **frequency cap** helps advertisers control repetition so campaigns can build recognition without creating saturation, fatigue, or unnecessary media waste.

In practice, frequency caps can be applied at different levels, including:

*   **Ad level:** Limiting exposure to a specific creative.
*   **Campaign level:** Controlling how often users see ads from one campaign.
*   **Line-item level:** Managing exposure within a specific buying tactic or placement.
*   **Audience level:** Adjusting exposure based on user behavior, intent, or funnel stage.
*   **Platform level:** Applying limits inside a DSP, social platform, CTV platform, or ad network.

The purpose is not to reduce reach blindly. It is to balance **reach, repetition, customer experience, and budget efficiency**. Too little exposure may weaken recall, while too much exposure can waste impressions and irritate the audience.

Frequency capping is especially important in [programmatic advertising](https://www.aidigital.com/blog/programmatic-advertising), where campaigns can run across many publishers, exchanges, devices, and formats at once. For cross-channel campaigns, frequency control also needs to be connected to measurement.

⚡️AI Digital’s guide, [**Cross-Channel Marketing Measurement: Challenges and Solutions**](http://www.aidigital.com/blog/cross-channel-marketing-measurement), explores how marketers evaluate duplicated reach and cumulative exposure across fragmented media environments.

### How a Frequency Cap Works

![Image 2: Frequency capping chart showing engagement across four visits, with Ad B introduced after the frequency cap while repeated exposure to Ad A leads to lower engagement.](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69a18e5fa71a1769128536f9/6a871e5a3c65bf33606e9c48_Frequency%20capping.webp)

_How a frequency cap works (Source)._

A **frequency cap** works by counting how many impressions have been served to a user or identifier within a selected timeframe. Once the user reaches the defined limit, the platform stops serving that ad or campaign to them until the cap resets.

For example, if a campaign has a cap of **three impressions per user per day**, the platform can show the ad up to three times in that daily window. After the third impression, that user becomes temporarily ineligible for the same campaign.

To enforce frequency limits, platforms rely on identifiers such as:

*   **Cookies** for browser-based environments.
*   **Device IDs** for mobile apps and connected devices.
*   **Authenticated IDs** from logged-in users.
*   **Household IDs** in some CTV and streaming environments.

_💡This process is easier inside one platform than across multiple systems. A DSP may recognize a user in programmatic display, but Meta, Google, Amazon, and CTV platforms may each apply their own frequency logic separately. To understand the buying infrastructure behind these controls, read AI Digital’s guide to_[_demand-side platforms_](https://www.aidigital.com/blog/demand-side-platform)_._

### Selecting the Right Timeframe

The timeframe determines how quickly a frequency cap resets. Choosing the wrong window can either limit campaign scale too aggressively or allow too much repeated exposure.

Common frequency cap windows include:

*   **Hourly caps:** Useful for high-volume campaigns where overexposure can happen quickly.
*   **Daily caps:** Common for display, social, video, and retargeting campaigns.
*   **Weekly caps:** Helpful for balancing reach and repetition in awareness or consideration campaigns.
*   **Monthly caps:** Useful for longer buying cycles, seasonal campaigns, or B2B audiences.
*   **Lifetime caps:** Best for preventing excessive exposure across the full campaign duration.

Shorter windows give advertisers tighter control over saturation, while longer windows support pacing across extended campaigns. For example, a daily cap may protect users from seeing the same retargeting ad too often, while a weekly cap may be better for broad brand awareness campaigns that need repeated exposure over time.

The right timeframe depends on campaign objective, audience size, creative rotation, purchase cycle, and channel mix. A narrow retargeting audience may need stricter controls, while a broad awareness campaign may tolerate more repetition if creative is varied and performance remains stable.

## Benefits of Frequency Capping

The main benefit of **frequency capping** is control. A campaign needs enough repetition to build memory, but too much exposure can create saturation, waste budget, and weaken the customer experience. A well-managed **frequency cap** helps advertisers find the point where repeated exposure still adds value without overwhelming the same audience.

For performance teams, frequency capping supports three practical goals:

*   **Protecting reach:** Budget is not over-concentrated on the same users.
*   **Reducing wasted impressions:** Ads stop serving once additional exposure is unlikely to improve outcomes.
*   **Improving customer experience:** Audiences are less likely to feel followed, interrupted, or irritated by the same brand.
*   **Maintaining campaign efficiency:** Marketers can monitor when frequency begins to hurt CTR, CPA, VTR, or conversion quality.

This matters because consumers are increasingly resistant to repetitive advertising. [Gartner’s](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-04-13-gartner-marketing-survey-finds-eighty-one-percent-of-consumers-tune-out-ads) 2026 consumer survey found that **81% of U.S. consumers try to ignore or tune out ads**, **52% actively take steps to block ads**, and **24% of Gen Z consumers say retargeted ads negatively affect their perception of the advertised brand**. That makes frequency management both a performance issue and a brand perception issue.

Frequency management should also connect to broader performance measurement. AI Digital’s

results.title: Use frequency capping - Google Ads Help
results.markdown:
Title: Use frequency capping - Google Ads Help

URL Source: https://support.google.com/adwords/answer/6034106

Final URL: https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6034106

Markdown Content:
Frequency capping allows you to limit the number of times ads appear to the same person. You can use frequency capping in Display campaigns and Video campaigns.

This article explains how to use frequency capping in your campaigns.

## How it works

Depending on your campaign type, frequency capping works differently.

### Display campaigns

*   You can allow Google Ads to optimize how often your ads show to users, or you can set a frequency cap manually to manage the number of impressions on the campaign, ad group, or ad.
*   Third-party cookies are used by default, but if those aren’t available, then first-party cookies are used to approximate impressions.
*   You can only use frequency capping from the "Frequency management" section in your campaign settings. You can’t adjust frequency capping settings when you create a new campaign.
*   For Display campaigns, only impressions that were viewable count toward frequency caps.

### Video campaigns

*   Frequency caps for Video campaigns can only be set on the campaign level. When you set the frequency cap for a Video campaign, you set a limit on your videos in a campaign for selected time intervals based on: 
    *   Impressions
    *   Views
    *   Both impressions and views

*   If the videos in a campaign are used in other Video campaigns, both those other impressions and views count towards the frequency cap of that campaign.
*   When a user reaches the frequency cap, Google stops showing this campaign to the user. This only applies to in-stream and bumper ads in the auction.

## Instructions

### Set a frequency cap in a Display campaign

**Note:** You can only set a frequency cap in a Display campaign after you create the campaign. This can be done from the "Frequency management" section in your campaign settings.

1.   Go to [**Campaigns**](https://ads.google.com/aw/campaigns) within the **Campaigns**![Image 1: Campaigns Icon](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/PYU3UjHzepAdY-dWS9ObIzq9WgLGS0SZeJS1hQ0Be3fxCIUQZaWCrR4HoYqriXSEbQ=w40) menu.
2.   Select **Settings** tab, then select a Display campaign you want to add a frequency cap to.
3.   Select**Additional settings**.
4.   Select **Frequency management** and then choose how often your ads show to the same user. You can choose to let Google Ads optimize how often your ads show (recommended) or choose your own settings for the frequency cap.
5.   Select**Save**.

### Set a frequency cap in a new Video campaign

1.   Go to [**Campaigns**](https://ads.google.com/aw/campaigns) within the **Campaigns**![Image 2: Campaigns Icon](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/PYU3UjHzepAdY-dWS9ObIzq9WgLGS0SZeJS1hQ0Be3fxCIUQZaWCrR4HoYqriXSEbQ=w40) menu.
2.   Select the plus button ![Image 3](https://storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/Ns5o4jgOAKaw8NnTPog3UMQHzmGiCUG3utl0) and select **New campaign**.
3.   Select your campaign objective and click **Continue**.
4.   Select your campaign type.
5.   Select**Continue**.
6.   Select**Additional settings**.
7.   Select **Frequency capping**. 
    *   **Cap impression frequency:** Limit how many times ads in this campaign can show to the same user.
    *   **Cap view frequency:** Limit how many times ads in this campaign can get a view or interaction from the same user.

8.   Enter the number of impressions or views cap for the campaign. The value must be a whole number (such as 4, not 4.5).
9.   Select a time interval (per day, week, or month).
10.   When you finish, select**Create campaign**.

### Set a frequency cap in an existing Video campaign

1.   Go to [**Campaigns**](https://ads.google.com/aw/campaigns) within the **Campaigns**![Image 4: Campaigns Icon](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/PYU3UjHzepAdY-dWS9ObIzq9WgLGS0SZeJS1hQ0Be3fxCIUQZaWCrR4HoYqriXSEbQ=w40) menu.
2.   Select **Settings** tab, then select the Video campaign you want to add a frequency cap to.
3.   Select**Additional settings**.
4.   Select **Frequency capping**. 
    *   **Cap impression frequency:** Limit how many times ads in this campaign can show to the same user.
    *   **Cap view frequency:** Limit how many times ads in this campaign can get a view or interaction from the same user.

5.   Enter the number of impressions or views cap for the campaign. The value must be a whole number (such as 4, not 4.5).
6.   Select a time interval (per day, week, or month).
7.   Select**Save**.

results.title: Explaining target frequency
results.markdown:
Title: Explaining target frequency

URL Source: https://ppc.land/target-frequency/

Published Time: 2026-10-16T18:49:17.000Z

Markdown Content:
Target frequency is a campaign setting in which an advertiser names the average number of times each person should see an ad over a fixed period, usually a week or a month, and the platform buys impressions to hit that average across as many people as possible. It exists because brand campaigns are planned around repetition: a single exposure is often judged too weak to be remembered, while a dozen in a week wastes money and irritates viewers. Rather than set an upper limit, target frequency makes the exposure level itself the goal. This article uses the term in that sense, as offered by Google Ads and Display & Video 360 (DV360) for YouTube and by Meta; older planning meanings are covered under disambiguation.

## How the goal is set and delivered

In Google Ads, **Target frequency** is a subtype of Video campaign. An advertiser chooses the objective "YouTube reach, views, and engagements", selects Video reach and then Target frequency, and enters a weekly or monthly number. According to Google's help centre, the permitted range depends on format. A multi-format campaign, which mixes skippable in-stream, bumper, in-feed and Shorts ads, accepts two to seven exposures per week or four to 12 per month. A campaign limited to non-skippable in-stream, or to skippable and bumper ads, accepts two to four per week or four to eight per month.

The system caps delivery so that heavy viewers do not absorb the budget, and pushes extra impressions at people below the target. Google states plainly that the setting "is not a frequency cap": some users will see an ad more often than the target in a given week to compensate for others who see it less. What the advertiser buys is an average, shaped into a narrow distribution, not a guarantee for each individual.

In the Google Ads API, a `TargetCpm` strategy carries a `target_frequency_goal` with two values: `target_count`, the number of exposures, and `time_unit`, which takes `WEEKLY` or `MONTHLY`. Reserved buys use a parallel structure on `FixedCpm`, where the goal is set to `TARGET_FREQUENCY`. The field first appeared in version 13 of the API; the Python client library carrying it was published on February 17, 2023, according to the Python Package Index.

In a simple example, a weekly target of three across 1 million adults needs about 3 million impressions; at a 6 euro cost per thousand impressions (CPM), that is 18,000 euros. With only 9,000 euros, the system holds frequency near three and reaches about half as many people. The target protects frequency, and reach absorbs the shortfall.

## Configuration rules and constraints

Google's documentation attaches a long list of conditions. A Target frequency campaign supports a single ad group, and existing campaigns cannot be converted. It runs on YouTube but not Google Video Partners, the third-party network. Bidding is by auction, with a target CPM set at ad group level, or by reservation for single-format campaigns. Content targeting by topic, keyword or placement is unavailable, as are shared budgets and political ads. Google recommends flights of two to four weeks, and at least seven days, without pausing or sharp budget moves near the end.

Google suggests at least as many distinct videos as the frequency target, so a weekly goal of four implies four creatives, to limit **wear-out**. Reporting centres on "average impression frequency per user (7 days)" and a frequency histogram, which can lag by up to 72 hours and excludes impressions of the same creative from other campaigns.

DV360 offers the same option inside a "YouTube & partners video" reach line item, with Target CPM as the only bid strategy. Line item frequency caps are switched off when it is used, but caps set at campaign, insertion order or cross-channel level still apply, and the stricter cap wins. According to DV360's help centre, a weekly target does not accumulate from one week to the next, while a monthly target, measured over 30 days or four weeks, builds cumulatively.

Meta handles the concept in two places. In **Reservation**, the fixed-price buying type that replaced Reach and Frequency in October 2023, target frequency is the default control and a hard frequency cap is the alternative, according to Jon Loomer, a Meta [advertising](https://ppc.land/target-frequency/#) consultant. Reservation requires a minimum reach of 200,000 people and is limited to Awareness and Engagement objectives. In auction buying, Meta began rolling out a weekly target for reach-optimised Awareness campaigns in late 2024, according to Loomer, requiring a lifetime budget, a flight of at least seven days and no bid controls.

## Origin and evolution

The idea predates digital media by decades. In 1972 Herbert Krugman, then at General Electric, published "Why Three Exposures May Be Enough" in the Journal of [Advertising](https://ppc.land/target-frequency/#) Research. Michael Naples gathered supporting evidence in Effective Frequency for the Association of National [Advertisers](https://ppc.land/target-frequency/#) in 1979, and three exposures per purchase cycle became television's planning default. Erwin Ephron challenged it in 1997, arguing that one exposure close to purchase can suffice.

Television planners could aim for a frequency level but not steer it person by person. Platforms with logged-in users could. Facebook was selling Reach and Frequency campaigns by 2016, with a 200,000-person minimum and fixed CPM pricing, according to a June 2016 description by Ignite Social Media.

Google launched Target frequency globally for YouTube on November 9, 2022, in a blog post by Marvin Renaud, director of global video solutions, and Ammar Ibrahim, group product manager for YouTube Ads. The initial maximum was four per week. Google said more than 95% of campaigns set up to its recommendations met their goal, based on 290 campaigns from 57 advertisers in the first half of 2022, and cited a Triscuit test at two per week that produced a 93% higher absolute ad recall lift than a non-optimised campaign. Both are Google's figures.

On December 2, 2024, DV360 announced [a monthly target for YouTube that optimises toward four to eight exposures](https://ppc.land/new-youtube-monthly-frequency-targets-differ-from-standard-frequency-capping/), and multi-format campaigns later widened the ranges to seven per week and 12 per month. On July 13, 2026, Google introduced **video campaign groups**, which apply one reach or frequency goal across several campaigns while each keeps its own budget. Google said DV360 support for coordinated goals across multiple YouTube line items was coming.

## Why it matters for marketers

Target frequency changes what a brand team buys. With a cap alone, frequency is an outcome checked after the fact. With a target, it is an input, and reach becomes the variable. Advertisers whose plans assume a set number of weekly exposures, often inherited from television, can buy against that assumption directly.

The setting sits inside a wider shift toward people-based measurement. Google began showing [frequency distribution and average frequency in Google Ads](https://ppc.land/google-introduces-frequency-distribution-and-average-frequency-in-google-ads/) in September 2020, with buckets from 1+ to 10+. DV360 [added 8+ and 9+ reach buckets on July 7, 2025](https://ppc.land/dv360-announces-major-reporting-changes-for-q3-2025/), filling the gap between 7+ and 10+, and on August 26, 2025 [replaced a bid-request frequency metric with cost-based savings metrics and Cost per reach](https://ppc.land/dv360-introduces-new-frequency-cap-and-reach-metrics/). PPC Land's [reach and frequency explainer](https://ppc.land/reach-and-frequency/) sets out how those numbers are built.

## Limitations and disputes

The central dispute is whether the target number is right. In February 2026, [Google's own researchers questioned frequency orthodoxy](https://ppc.land/google-researchers-question-advertising-frequency-orthodoxy-in-new-analysis/), arguing that the first impact delivers the most value and that a second contact is usually worth more when it reaches a new person. They cited YouTube Brand Lift data indexing second impacts at 1.5 to 1.8, below the 2.0 that would make them as valuable as a first. Yet the July 2026 campaign groups announcement cited a Google Meridian marketing mix modelling study of about 600 US brands, using data from 2023 to 2025, that put optimal frequency at 2.7 per week and linked it to a 19% lift in return on investment. Both positions come from Google, and they point in different directions.

Title: CTV Frequency Management Strategy: Optimize Ad Exposure for Maximum ROI

## CTV Frequency Management Strategy: Optimize Ad Exposure for Maximum ROI

Connected TV advertising delivers the highest viewability rates in digital marketing—but only when frequency is managed correctly. Brands that optimize frequency management see 35-45% better cost efficiency and 20-30% higher conversion rates compared to unmanaged campaigns.

Here's the complete framework for building frequency strategies that maximize CTV performance while preventing ad fatigue.

## The CTV Frequency Challenge

Unlike traditional TV where frequency control was nearly impossible, CTV offers precise frequency management—but most advertisers aren't using it strategically.

**The problem:**

*   68% of CTV campaigns run without proper frequency caps
*   Average viewer sees the same ad 8-12 times before taking action
*   Frequency tolerance varies dramatically by product category and audience segment
*   Poor frequency management wastes 25-40% of CTV budgets

**The opportunity:** Brands with sophisticated frequency strategies achieve 3-5x better efficiency than those using platform defaults.

## Understanding CTV Frequency Dynamics

### Viewer Behavior Patterns

**CTV Consumption Habits:**

*   Average viewer watches 3.2 hours of CTV daily
*   78% of viewing happens during 3-4 consistent time blocks
*   Household sharing means individual frequency is often underestimated
*   Cross-device viewing complicates true frequency measurement

**Frequency Tolerance by Category:**

*   **High consideration purchases (automobiles, luxury):** 12-15 exposures optimal
*   **Mid-funnel DTC (supplements, skincare):** 6-8 exposures peak performance
*   **Impulse purchases (food, fashion):** 3-5 exposures before diminishing returns
*   **B2B products:** 15-20 exposures due to longer decision cycles

### The Frequency Sweet Spot

**Research-Backed Optimization:** Our analysis of 500+ CTV campaigns reveals the frequency effectiveness curve:

*   **1-3 exposures:** Awareness building, low conversion rates
*   **4-6 exposures:** Peak conversion efficiency for most DTC categories
*   **7-10 exposures:** Sustained performance with slight efficiency decline
*   **11+ exposures:** Rapid efficiency drop, increased ad fatigue

## Strategic Frequency Management Framework

### Phase 1: Audience Segmentation for Frequency

**High-Value Frequency Segments:**

*   **New prospects:** Higher frequency tolerance (8-12 exposures)
*   **Previous website visitors:** Mid-range frequency (5-8 exposures)
*   **Past purchasers:** Lower frequency for retention campaigns (3-5 exposures)
*   **High LTV customers:** Premium frequency allocation (10-15 exposures)

**Demographic Frequency Variations:**

*   **Age 25-34:** Higher tolerance, accept 7-9 exposures
*   **Age 35-54:** Moderate tolerance, optimize for 5-7 exposures
*   **Age 55+:** Lower tolerance, cap at 4-6 exposures
*   **High-income households:** Greater tolerance for premium brand messaging

### Phase 2: Creative Rotation Strategy

**The Creative Fatigue Solution:** Instead of limiting frequency, rotate creative to maintain engagement:

**3-Creative Rotation Model:**

*   **Awareness creative (Exposures 1-3):** Problem identification and brand introduction
*   **Consideration creative (Exposures 4-6):** Product benefits and social proof
*   **Conversion creative (Exposures 7-9):** Strong CTA with urgency or offer

**5-Creative Advanced Model:** For high-frequency campaigns, expand creative variety:

*   Educational content
*   Customer testimonials
*   Product demonstrations
*   Competitive comparisons
*   Limited-time offers

### Phase 3: Dynamic Frequency Optimization

**Real-Time Adjustment Triggers:**

*   **Performance decline:** Reduce frequency when CPA increases 25%+
*   **Creative fatigue indicators:** Swap creative when CTR drops 30%+
*   **Audience saturation:** Expand targeting when frequency exceeds thresholds
*   **Budget pacing:** Increase frequency when under-delivering on impressions

## Technical Implementation Guide

### Platform-Specific Frequency Controls

**The Trade Desk:**

```
Campaign Level: Set overall frequency cap (7-day window)
Ad Group Level: Granular frequency by audience segment
Creative Level: Sequential creative rotation setup
```

**Amazon DSP:**

```
Line Item Settings: Frequency cap by household/device
Audience Targeting: Layer frequency rules by customer segment
Creative Management: Automated creative rotation by exposure count
```

**Google DV360:**

```
Insertion Order: Master frequency cap across all line items
Line Item: Segment-specific frequency management
Creative Assignment: Sequential messaging by frequency bucket
```

### Frequency Cap Configuration

**Recommended Starting Points:**

*   **Awareness campaigns:** 8 exposures per 7-day window
*   **Conversion campaigns:** 5 exposures per 7-day window
*   **Retargeting campaigns:** 12 exposures per 30-day window
*   **Brand consideration:** 6 exposures per 14-day window

**Advanced Configuration:**

```
Daily Cap: 2 exposures maximum
Weekly Cap: 5-8 exposures (varies by campaign objective)
Monthly Cap: 15-20 exposures for long-term brand building
Creative Level Cap: 3 exposures before rotation required
```

## Measurement and Optimization

### Essential Frequency Metrics

**Primary KPIs:**

*   **Average frequency per campaign and audience segment**
*   **Cost efficiency by frequency bucket (1-3, 4-6, 7-9, 10+ exposures)**
*   **Creative fatigue indicators (CTR decline over time)**
*   **Conversion rate by frequency exposure**

**Advanced Metrics:**

*   **Incremental reach vs. frequency trade-offs**
*   **Cross-device frequency measurement**
*   **Household vs. individual frequency impact**
*   **Brand lift by frequency segment**

### Frequency Performance Analysis

**Weekly Optimization Reviews:**

1.   **Segment Performance:** Analyze conversion rates by frequency bucket
2.   **Creative Fatigue Assessment:** Identify declining performance indicators
3.   **Reach vs. Frequency Optimization:** Adjust budget allocation for optimal balance
4.   **Competitive Frequency Analysis:** Monitor category frequency trends

**Monthly Strategy Adjustments:**

1.   **Frequency Cap Optimization:** Test increased/decreased caps based on performance
2.   **Creative Strategy Evolution:** Expand or condense creative rotation based on fatigue data
3.   **Audience Frequency Segmentation:** Refine frequency targets by customer value
4.   **Cross-Campaign Frequency Management:** Coordinate frequency across multiple campaigns

## Budget Allocation by Frequency Strategy

### Reach vs. Frequency Budget Models

**Reach-Focused Allocation (60/40):**

*   60% budget allocated to new audience reach (frequency cap: 4-5)
*   40% budget for frequency building with high-value segments (frequency cap: 8-10)
*   Best for: Brand awareness campaigns, new product launches

**Frequency-Focused Allocation (40/60):**

*   40% budget for broad reach (frequency cap: 3-4)
*   60% budget for deep frequency with qualified audiences (frequency cap: 10-12)
*   Best for: Conversion campaigns, consideration-heavy products

**Balanced Model (50/50):**

*   50% reach optimization with moderate frequency (frequency cap: 5-6)
*   50% frequency optimization with targeted segments (frequency cap: 8-9)
*   Best for: Full-funnel campaigns, consistent brand building

## Advanced Frequency Strategies

### Sequential Creative Messaging

**Story Arc Development:** Create connected creative narratives that build across frequency exposures:

**Exposure 1-2:** Problem introduction and emotional connection **Exposure 3-4:** Solution presentation and product introduction  
**Exposure 5-6:** Benefit demonstration and proof points **Exposure 7-8:** Social proof and customer testimonials **Exposure 9-10:** Strong call-to-action with urgency or incentive

### Cross-Device Frequency Coordination

**Household Frequency Management:**

*   Implement household-level frequency caps across all connected devices
*   Use deterministic matching to prevent over-exposure across TVs, tablets, phones
*   Coordinate frequency between CTV and linear TV campaigns for unified household reach

**Platform Integration:**

*   Share frequency data between CTV and social media platforms
*   Coordinate frequency caps across Google (YouTube + DV360) and Meta (Facebook + Instagram)
*   Use first-party data to manage frequency across owned and paid channels

### Seasonal Frequency Adjustments

**Holiday Campaign Optimization:**

*   **Pre-holiday (October-November):** Higher frequency tolerance due to gift planning
*   **Peak holiday (December):** Reduce frequency as ad saturation increases across category
*   **Post-holiday (January-February):** Minimum frequency as consumers experience ad fatigue

*   **Q1:** Conserv

results.markdown:
Title: What is frequency capping | AppsFlyer mobile glossary

URL Source: https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/

Markdown Content:
Frequency capping is an online advertising technique that limits the number of times an ad is shown to the same user to prevent fatigue.

Frequency capping is an online advertising technique that controls how often a single user sees an ad. It balances ad exposure with audience engagement.

With frequency limits, you avoid annoying your audience, protect engagement, preserve brand perception, and prevent wasted [ad spend](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/ad-spend/). Caps ensure ads remain fresh and relevant, reaching new potential customers rather than retargeting the same users excessively.

## [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)Why is frequency capping important?

It’s never a good idea to blow through your ad budgets without any control over who sees your campaigns and how often they see them. Here are a few reasons why frequency capping is essential for your online ad campaigns:

### [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)1. Prevent irritation and fatigue

When audiences see the same ad over and over, they get bored and stop paying attention — a phenomenon known as ad fatigue. Constant repetition can also get pretty irritating.

Frequency caps prevent over-serving the same audience. Consumers are becoming more intolerant of advertising, with [64% of US adults](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1441101/frequency-ad-avoidance-adults-united-states-medium/)saying they spend extra time finding ways to avoid ads on free-with-ads video platforms like YouTube and Hulu.

### [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)2. Extend your campaign longevity

Limiting ad frequency can help spread your impressions over a longer period of time without losing effectiveness. This also encourages advertisers to use more variety in ad creatives.

### [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)3. Optimize ad budgets

Frequency capping adds control to help stretch your dollar. It ensures your budget is spent targeting new audiences instead of showing ads repeatedly to the same users. By managing ad frequency by placement, time of day, and day of the week, you gain greater control over your ads’ effectiveness.

## [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)How does frequency capping work?

Frequency capping is a common feature offered by [ad networks](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/ad-network/) like Google Ads, Meta Ads, and [programmatic](https://www.appsflyer.com/resources/guides/programmatic-advertising/)ad platforms. Some [demand-side platforms (DSPs)](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/demand-side-platform/) also provide frequency capping.

There are three elements to consider when setting caps:

*   Frequency — how many times to show an ad to a user
*   Creative — which creative or campaign should be limited
*   Timeframe — how long the cap should be in place

Ad platforms track how often an ad or campaign is shown to the same users using unique identifiers like cookies, [device IDs](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/device-id/), or tracking pixels. Before serving the ad, the platform checks the frequency cap to see if the limit the advertiser sets is reached. If not, the ad is served, and the impression is logged within milliseconds to maintain a seamless user experience.

## [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)The impact of cookie deprecation

Frequency capping hinges on identifying the user and checking if they’ve seen the ad previously. But times are changing in the industry. With increasing privacy regulations like [Apple’s ATT](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/app-tracking-transparency/) framework and cookie deprecation, ad networks are finding new ways to fill the data gap.

Mobile advertisers are shifting from relying on device-level tracking that identifies specific users to more aggregated data and probabilistic modeling. Mobile measurement partners (like AppsFlyer) effectively use [probabilistic modeling](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/probabilistic-modeling/) as a fallback method when unique IDs are unavailable, employing machine learning to estimate user behavior based on large data sets and aggregated insights.

## [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)How to set the right frequency cap

While setting frequency caps from the start of your campaign is a good idea, always check your data to get them right. Here are the key metrics to guide you.

**Ad schedule performance:**On platforms like Google Ads and Meta Ads, you can check what time or day of the week your ads are most effective. Consider day or time capping based on this report.

**Conversion rate:**Compare [conversion rates](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/conversion-rate/) across users who saw the ad multiple times. If conversions drop significantly after a certain number of views, it’s a sign that frequency capping may help improve efficiency.

**Frequency:** High ad frequency with low conversion rates could indicate that your ads are no longer connecting with users. It may be time to limit that creative to prevent fatigue.

**Impressions:** Review the total impressions to understand how often your ads are shown. High impressions with low engagement indicate ad fatigue.

**Click-through rate (CTR):**Declining [CTR](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/ctr/) over time may signal ad fatigue and a need to refresh your creatives. What initially grabbed attention has become wallpaper.

## [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)Best practices for frequency capping

Your ad campaigns should objectively be measured by total impact, as frequency directly influences brand lift. You can maximize campaign potential by tailoring frequency to specific market, message, and media factors — there’s no one-size-fits-all approach.

As a good starting point, Meta’s research condenses the “best practices” of frequency capping into one handy chart.

This chart outlines the various market, message, and media factors that influence frequency capping:

*   **Lower frequency**: Ideal for established brands with high market share, long purchase cycles, unique messages, and multiple media channels. Suitable for continuous or long-duration campaigns in low-season periods.
*   **Higher frequency:**Recommended for new brands with low market share, short purchase cycles, and frequent usage. Applies to complex or less unique messages, new campaigns, short-duration, high-season campaigns, or single-channel (such as Facebook-only) strategies.

Here are some further tips to help you make frequency capping work for you:

### [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)Rotate creatives

Crafting a lot of good creatives can be resource-intensive, but it’s a worthwhile investment. When there’s more variation between creatives within one campaign, your audience is less likely to experience ad fatigue across the board. It’s not always about how many different creatives you have, but the distinct variety between them.

### [](https://www.appsflyer.com/glossary/frequency-capping/)Not all impressions are created equal

Not every impression is worth the same. Some ad placements may have lower visibility and be more crowded than others, hence making your impressions less effective. Platforms with multiple placements, high ad density, or overlapping audiences can increase exposure, leading to higher frequency. Engaging placements may need less frequency to be effective, while less engaging spots must be shown more often.

## Key takeaways

*   Frequency capping is an online advertising technique that limits how often a single user sees an ad, helping prevent ad fatigue.
*   Frequency capping prevents user irritation, extends campaign longevity by spreading impressions over time, and optimizes budgets by preventing overspending on the same audience.
*   Ad platforms use unique identifiers like cookies or device IDs to track impressions per user and enforce frequency limits in real time, maintaining a seamless experience.
*   With cookie deprecation and privacy rules, platforms are shifting to probabilistic modeling and aggregated data, enabling marketers to approximate frequency control without identifying individual users.
*   Adjust frequency caps based on market, message, and media factors. Other best practices include regularly analyzing performance metrics like CTR and conversion rate, and rotating ad creatives to maintain audience interest and prevent fatigue.
